content.title: About
content.content: Unsweetened applesauce is a 100 % pure puree made from ripe apples, prepared without added sugar, sweeteners, or preservatives. It has a smooth texture and a mildly tart flavor, suitable for both children and adults.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Applesauce is often used as a first solid food for infants after breast‑milk or formula.
In the United States and Canada, applesauce is a common component of school lunch programs.
Unsweetened varieties retain most of the vitamins and dietary fiber found in fresh apples.
Apples are among the world’s most widely cultivated fruits, with over 80 million tonnes of puree produced annually.
The production process involves heat treatment that eliminates pathogens while preserving the apple aroma.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Applesauce provides vitamin C, which supports the immune system and aids collagen synthesis.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: The puree retains pectin and fiber that promote healthy digestion and help regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: Without added sugar, applesauce contains about 45 kcal per 100 g, making it suitable for calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Flavonoids and polyphenols in apples help combat free radicals.

items.title: Supports cardiovascular health
items.content: Pectin may help lower LDL (bad) cholesterol levels.

items.title: Apple allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may experience allergic reactions to apples, ranging from itching to swelling or hives.

items.title: Natural sugar content
items.content: Although no sugar is added, the puree contains natural fruit sugars, which should be considered by people with diabetes.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: The acidic pH can irritate a sensitive stomach in some individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Unsweetened applesauce can be enjoyed on its own, mixed into oatmeal, yogurt, smoothies, baked goods, or used as a base for sauces and desserts. For infants, it is often served slightly warmed.

content.title: Storage
content.content: After opening, keep the puree in a sealed container in the refrigerator and consume within 7 days. Unopened packages should be stored in a cool, dry place away from direct light.

content.title: About
content.content: Avocado dressing is a creamy sauce made from ripe avocado, olive oil, lime juice, and spices. It has a mild nutty flavor, a subtle tang, and a silky texture, making it perfect for salads, sandwiches, and seafood dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Avocado contains more monounsaturated fats than most fruits.
The sauce originates from Mexico, where avocado is used in guacamole.
Lime juice not only adds flavor but also prevents avocado from browning.
The dressing can be kept in the refrigerator for up to 5 days without losing taste or texture.
Vegans often use it as a mayo alternative.

items.title: Rich in healthy fats
items.content: Monounsaturated fatty acids support heart health and help lower LDL cholesterol.

items.title: Source of vitamin E
items.content: Vitamin E acts as an antioxidant, protecting cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Contains potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate blood pressure and supports muscle function.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Fiber from avocado promotes regular bowel movements.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The dressing provides folate and vitamin B6, important for metabolism.

items.title: Avocado allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to avocado.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: Because of the oil, the dressing is relatively calorie‑dense; portion control is advised.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: Avocado contains oxalates, which can contribute to kidney stone formation in susceptible people.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Use the dressing as a salad topping, spread on toast, dip for vegetables, or drizzle over grilled fish and chicken. It also blends well into smoothies for a creamy texture.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the dressing in an airtight container in the refrigerator at +4 °C. Exposure to air may cause darkening; add a splash of lime juice to slow the process. Consume within 5 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Provolone is a semi‑hard Italian cheese made from cow’s milk. The reduced‑fat version has a portion of the butterfat removed, making it lower in calories while retaining its characteristic nutty flavor and aroma.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Provolone is traditionally used as a melting cheese for casseroles and sandwiches.
The cheese is named after the town of Provolone in Italy, where it was first produced in the 19th century.
Reduced‑fat provolone appeared in the 1970s in response to growing demand for low‑fat dairy products.
It is often used as a mozzarella substitute on pizza because it melts more smoothly.
The cheese can be aged up to 6 months, developing a richer taste over time.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Reduced‑fat provolone provides about 28 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: Low fat content
items.content: Fat typically does not exceed 5 g per 100 g, making it suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Calcium and phosphorus
items.content: The cheese is a good source of calcium and phosphorus, essential for bone and tooth health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Provolone contains riboflavin (B2) and vitamin B12, which aid energy metabolism.

items.title: Probiotic properties
items.content: Like most aged cheeses, provolone contains live cultures that can support a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Although aged cheeses have lower lactose, people with severe intolerance may still experience symptoms.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: The cheese can contain up to 600 mg of sodium per 100 g, which should be considered by those with hypertension.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to casein, the main milk protein.

items.title: Shelf‑life control
items.content: Improper storage can lead to mold growth, rendering the cheese unsafe to eat.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Reduced‑fat provolone works well in casseroles, pizza, pasta, sandwiches, and salads. Slice it thin, grate it, or melt it as a top layer on hot dishes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the cheese in its original packaging or an airtight container in the refrigerator at 2–4 °C. For longer storage (over 2 weeks), wrap it in wax paper followed by aluminum foil to prevent drying. Do not keep at room temperature for more than 4 hours.

coffee-pre-lightened-and-pre-sweetened-w.title: Coffee, pre‑lightened and pre‑sweetened with low‑calorie sweetener

content.title: About
content.content: Coffee, pre‑lightened and pre‑sweetened with a low‑calorie sweetener, is a ready‑to‑drink product. The beans are lightly roasted and then a low‑calorie sweetener (5215) is added during processing. The result is an aromatic, mildly sweet beverage with minimal calories.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Light roasting preserves more chlorogenic acids, which have antioxidant properties.
Low‑calorie sweetener 5215 is usually based on stevia or erythritol and does not raise blood sugar.
Pre‑lightened coffee dissolves faster in hot water than traditional dark roast.
It is popular in fitness and diet plans for controlling calorie intake.
Light‑roasted coffee offers brighter acidity and fruity notes.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: The light roast retains polyphenols that help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Energy boost
items.content: Caffeine improves focus and increases alertness without a sudden crash.

items.title: Low calorie
items.content: Sweetener 5215 adds sweetness without significantly increasing the drink’s calorie count.

items.title: Supports blood sugar control
items.content: Absence of sugar and use of a low‑calorie sweetener help maintain stable glucose levels.

items.title: Metabolism support
items.content: Caffeine can slightly raise metabolic rate, aiding fat burning.

items.title: Caffeine sensitivity
items.content: Some individuals may experience anxiety, insomnia, or rapid heartbeat.

items.title: Possible gastrointestinal irritation
items.content: Consuming too quickly can cause heartburn or stomach upset.

items.title: Allergy to sweetener
items.content: Rarely, individuals may have an intolerance to components of sweetener 5215.

items.title: Drug interactions
items.content: Caffeine may amplify the effects of stimulants and reduce the efficacy of sedatives.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Dissolve 1‑2 teaspoons of the product in hot (not boiling) water and stir until fully dissolved. Optionally add milk, plant‑based alternatives, or spices such as cinnamon or cardamom. Suitable for cold brew, lattes, and protein shakes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a dry, cool place in a tightly sealed container, protected from moisture and direct sunlight. For extended shelf life, keep refrigerated to preserve aroma and prevent clumping.

content.title: About
content.content: Beef liver is the organ meat of cattle, packed with nutrients. It has a tender, slightly bitter flavor and a soft texture when cooked. Liver is a staple in many traditional cuisines and can be pan‑fried, stewed, baked, or made into pâtés.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Beef liver is one of the most concentrated sources of vitamin A in foods.
In the 19th century liver was considered “food for the strong” and was a common part of athletes’ and laborers’ diets.
The iron in liver is in the highly bioavailable heme form, easier for the body to absorb than plant iron.
In some cultures liver is served as a delicacy, but unlike foie gras it does not require special fattening of the animal.
Liver loses nutrients quickly after slaughter, so it is best eaten fresh.

items.title: Rich in vitamin A
items.content: Vitamin A supports vision, immune function, and skin health.

items.title: High in iron
items.content: Heme iron helps form hemoglobin and prevents anemia.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Liver provides B12, riboflavin, niacin, and folate, essential for energy metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Liver offers complete protein needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Contains copper and zinc
items.content: These minerals support enzyme function, immunity, and wound healing.

items.title: High vitamin A content
items.content: Excessive liver consumption can lead to hypervitaminosis A, especially in pregnant women.

items.title: Cholesterol level
items.content: Liver is relatively high in cholesterol; people with hypercholesterolemia should limit intake.

items.title: Contamination risk
items.content: Liver can accumulate toxins and heavy metals, so choose products from reputable sources.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to beef liver.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Liver can be quickly sautéed with onions, made into pâté, added to stews or soups. Before cooking, rinse it, remove any membranes, and cut into bite‑size pieces. For a milder taste, many chefs marinate liver in milk or lemon juice.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh beef liver in the refrigerator at 0‑2 °C in an airtight container for up to 2 days. For longer storage, freeze it at –18 °C, where it keeps quality for about 3 months. Before use, check for an off‑odor – a sour or rancid smell indicates spoilage.

content.title: About
content.content: Mutton tallow is the rendered fat of sheep (mutton or lamb), a hard, white-to-cream fat with a strong, distinctive flavor. It includes fat from the tail of fat-tailed sheep, which is widely used in Central Asian, Middle Eastern, and Caucasian cooking. Mutton tallow is used for frying, in pilaf and stews, and to give dishes a rich meaty flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Fat-tailed sheep store fat in their tails, and tail fat is prized in Central Asian, Middle Eastern, and Caucasian cuisines.
Mutton tallow is firm at room temperature and melts at a higher temperature than beef fat.
It is a traditional cooking fat for dishes such as pilaf, kebabs, and dumplings in Central Asia.
It has a strong, distinctive sheep flavor that differs from beef fat or poultry fat.
Rendering the fat means slowly melting it and straining out the solids.

items.title: Concentrated energy
items.content: Mutton tallow is a calorie-dense source of energy.

items.title: Heat-stable for cooking
items.content: It suits high-heat cooking such as frying and browning meat.

items.title: Adds flavor
items.content: A little tallow gives dishes a rich, traditional flavor.

items.title: Contains fat-soluble vitamins
items.content: Mutton fat contains small amounts of vitamins A, D, E, and K, depending on the animal's diet.

items.title: Traditional cooking fat
items.content: It is a staple ingredient in several traditional cuisines.

items.title: Very high in saturated fat
items.content: Mutton tallow is very high in saturated fat, and health organizations generally recommend limiting saturated fat, especially for heart health.

items.title: Cholesterol and calories
items.content: Mutton tallow contains cholesterol and is calorie-dense, so portions should be small.

items.title: Strong flavor and overheating
items.content: Its strong taste is not liked by everyone, and heating it past its smoke point or reusing it many times can produce harmful compounds.

items.title: Spoilage
items.content: Mutton tallow can turn rancid if stored improperly.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Mutton tallow is used in small amounts to fry onions and meat for pilaf, stews, and dumplings, or to brown meat and vegetables. It is melted until hot but not smoking. Use it sparingly and balance heavy dishes with vegetables and salads.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store rendered mutton tallow in an airtight container in a cool, dark place or in the refrigerator, where it keeps for several months, or freeze it for longer storage. Raw fat should be refrigerated and used within a few days. Discard tallow that smells rancid or sour.

content.title: About
content.content: A sweet cinnamon roll is a soft yeasted dough swirled with a fragrant cinnamon filling and served without frosting. It is a classic treat in Scandinavian and American cuisines, often enjoyed with tea or coffee.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The original cinnamon roll, called kanelbulle, originated in Sweden.
In the United States, National Cinnamon Roll Day is celebrated on October 4th.
The dough is typically made with milk, butter, and eggs, giving it a tender, airy texture.
The filling usually contains ground cinnamon, sugar, and sometimes nuts or raisins.
Without frosting, the roll showcases the natural flavors of the dough and spice.

items.title: Source of fiber
items.content: Whole‑grain dough provides dietary fiber that supports digestive health.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Cinnamon is rich in polyphenols, which may help reduce oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports blood sugar balance
items.content: Some studies suggest cinnamon can aid in stabilizing blood glucose levels.

items.title: Quick energy boost
items.content: Carbohydrates in the dough supply fast‑acting energy, making it a convenient morning snack.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Yeast‑leavened dough contains B1, B2, and B3 vitamins important for metabolism.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: The sweet filling can raise the calorie count and affect blood sugar.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Traditional dough contains wheat, making it unsuitable for people with celiac disease.

items.title: Calorie dense
items.content: Butter and sugar make the roll calorie‑rich, so portion control is advised.

items.title: Excess cinnamon
items.content: Large amounts of cinnamon may irritate the stomach in sensitive individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the roll warm, sliced in half. It pairs well with coffee, tea, or milk. For extra richness, add a pat of butter or a sprinkle of nuts.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 2 days. For longer storage, refrigerate (up to 5 days) or freeze (up to 2 months). Warm before serving in the oven or microwave.

content.title: About
content.content: Turnip is a root vegetable from the Brassicaceae family, cultivated in temperate regions. Raw turnip has a crisp texture, a mildly peppery and refreshing flavor, and a pale white or pinkish flesh. It is commonly used in salads, as a crunchy snack, or as a side dish.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Turnip belongs to the same family as cabbage, broccoli, and mustard.
There are over 200 turnip varieties, differing in color, shape, and pungency.
Historically, turnips were used in folk medicine to aid digestion.
Turnips grow quickly – from sowing to harvest usually takes 3–4 weeks.
The edible part is the swollen stem base, not a true root like carrots.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Turnip provides a high amount of vitamin C, which supports the immune system and collagen synthesis.

items.title: Low‑calorie food
items.content: With very few calories per serving, turnip is an excellent choice for weight‑controlled diets.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber in turnip aids digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Contains potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate fluid balance and supports heart function.

items.title: Antioxidant compounds
items.content: Phenolic compounds in turnip have antioxidant properties that protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to turnip, such as skin rash or swelling.

items.title: Gas formation
items.content: Consuming large amounts of turnip can cause bloating due to its raffinose content.

items.title: Medication interactions
items.content: High vitamin C levels may enhance the effect of certain drugs, for example anticoagulants.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Raw turnip is usually washed, trimmed, and eaten whole, sliced into rounds, or cut into matchsticks. It can be added to salads, sandwiches, snack plates, or used as a garnish.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store turnip in the refrigerator in a perforated bag or a container with a damp cloth to keep it crisp for up to 2 weeks. Rinse thoroughly before consumption.
